Authors: D. Jude, I. Ekengwu, A. Ilechukwu, S. C. Anyaora, Augustine Uzochukwu Mmadumere
Title: Machine Learning for Process Optimization and Defect Detection in Metal Additive Manufacturing: A Critical Review of Algorithms, In-Situ Monitoring Strategies, and Quality Assurance Frameworks
Source: Journal of Mechanical Engineering and Manufacturing
Abstract: Among the many manufacturing technologies to emerge in the last three decades, metal additive manufacturing (AM)—spanning laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), directed energy deposition (DED), and electron beam melting (EBM)—stands out for the speed and breadth of its industrial adoption. Once confined to producing plastic concept models, it now fabricates flight-critical aerospace structures, load-bearing skeletal implants, and thermally demanding heat management components. Yet persistent process-induced defects—among them gas porosity, lack-of-fusion voids, hot cracking, and inter-layer delamination—continue to jeopardize part integrity and create formidable barriers to certification in regulated sectors. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have attracted growing attention as remedies, offering the capacity to extract decision-relevant patterns from the rich multi-modal data streams that flow continuously during metal AM builds. This review undertakes a critical examination of the current state of ML-driven process optimization and defect detection for metal AM. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are evaluated for image-based anomaly identification; long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and transformer architectures are assessed for temporal process monitoring; reinforcement learning is examined for closed-loop parameter governance; and generative adversarial networks are considered as instruments for training data augmentation. In-situ monitoring hardware—encompassing melt-pool cameras, pyrometers, acoustic emission sensors, and photodiode arrays—is surveyed alongside the sensor fusion strategies that sharpen defect localization performance. Closed-loop quality assurance architectures, digital twin integration, and ML-guided parameter optimization receive detailed critical evaluation. Drawing on a systematic synthesis of more than 130 peer-reviewed studies spanning 2016 to 2025, we identify structural gaps: a shortage of large annotated benchmark datasets, insufficient cross-domain generalization, and the computational demands of real-time industrial deployment. A forward-looking research roadmap—centred on physics-informed neural networks, federated learning architectures, and edge-optimized inference—is advanced as the route toward certifiable, industrially viable ML quality assurance systems for metal AM.

Authors: S. Meitner, L. Baylor
Title: Initial Commissioning Test Results of the Wendelstein 7-X Continuous Pellet Fueling System
Abstract: Abstract A continuous pellet fueling system (CPFS) for use on the Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) stellarator has been fabricated and assembled with commissioning tests completed at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). Continuous fueling is accomplished by cutting pellets from the cross section of a continuous solid extrusion produced by a twin-screw extruder and accelerated by a gas gun cutter mechanism. The pellets travel through a series of straight guide tubes before entering the stellarator through a curved guide tube. The CPFS has an array of diagnostics that include the extruder torque, rotation rate, and thrust. A shock and pressure sensor provide verification of proper pellet cutting and acceleration. Two ORNL-developed microwave cavity diagnostics within the injection line guide tubes provide pellet speed and relative mass measurements. For commissioning, a high-speed camera has been positioned at the base of the extruder to verify extrusion speed and quality as well as the pellet cutting process, and a third microwave cavity has been mounted after the curved guide tube to verify pellet quality and size. Maximum injection rate, pellet speed, barrel and guide tube induced erosion, and pellet survivability data have been recorded. This paper presents the laboratory experimental setup and results of these commissioning tests.

Authors: Qi-Long Yang, Jin-Xia Liu, Yan Shi, Yan-Wei Wang, H. Men
Title: MDFE-Net: A Meta-Learning Driven Dual-Branch Feature Extraction Network for E-Nose Sensor Drift Adaptation.
Abstract: Gas sensors are prone to ageing, environmental fluctuations, and device-to-device variability during long-term deployment. The resulting sensor drift progressively erodes the recognition performance of Electronic nose (E-nose) systems. Here, a Meta-learning Driven Dual-branch Feature Extraction E-nose Drift Adaptation Network (MDFE-Net) was developed for few-shot drift compensation. A dual-branch feature extraction module (DBFE) was constructed to encode temporal dynamics and cross-sensor spatial response patterns, enabling discriminative feature-level modelling of drifted samples. Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) was incorporated to learn task-shared priors and to enable rapid adaptation to unseen drift conditions with only a few labelled samples. An adaptive triplet loss and a dynamically reweighted cross-entropy loss were used to tighten intra-class clusters and enlarge inter-class margins. MDFE-Net achieves 95.53% accuracy under long-term drift and 95.71% accuracy under short-term drift on the Gas Sensor Array Drift Dataset. It maintains 97.89% accuracy under cross-device evaluation on the Twin Gas Sensor Arrays benchmark. Together, MDFE-Net couples deep metric learning with meta-learning to mitigate long-term nonlinear drift and improve cross-device generalisation when calibration labels are scarce.

Authors: R. Sudhakar
Title: Robust Digital Twin Approach Towards Operational Excellence and Sustainability Goals
Abstract: The objective of this paper is to provide new insights and best practices towards the digital twin concepts, particularly in the oil and gas sector and the potential benefits towards achieving the operational excellence and sustainability goals. By using the digital twin technology for asset management, reservoir management, process optimization and training and simulation, the operating companies not only improve efficiency, reduce costs, and achieve operational excellence, more importantly it can also optimize the operations and reduce GHG emissions. The digital twin concept helps in creating a digital replica of the physical assets and the associated processes. This technology can transform the way the oil and gas industry operate, enabling to achieve the operations excellence. As every field produces enormous amount of data which comes from sensors and field automation, the same can be leveraged through a digital twin that can support right from the conceptual design and various other phases of a field development capital project till operations and maintenance up to the retirement of the field and its associated assets. This paper looks in detail at the various approaches wherein the operating companies with their digital information and management system at organization level, can augment such Enterprise level digital twin methodologies. It also addresses the various process of Statement of Requirements (SOR), Data sources analysis, Modelling of the digital twins, Scenario analysis, and Implementation and continuous monitoring and improvement. This paper utilizes the various lessons learned and real time scenarios correlated with specific applications in the upstream oil and gas facilities. The results perceived, noticeably identify the importance for adopting the approach in a structured way rather than starting at the random stages while arraying the Digital twin journey. It further scrutinizes the digital twin solution architecture which can fit within the current organization wide enterprise domain, and also the latent and resultant advantages of implementation within premises or in a cloud environment. Another key aspect in this strategy was to develop the requirement standard for the Digital twin at enterprise level for existing assets and new development fields. In addition, it highlights the application specific scenarios which can be considered prototypical in implementation of this technology in the oil and gas industry having the potential to improve operational and sustainability performance and minimize environmental impact. Lastly, it concludes with the accompanying challenges to ensure that the digital twin solution is cyber secure and compliant while integrating with existing / new control systems such as DCS/ICSS and ERP to provide a comprehensive view of the physical entity's performance and to support effective decision-making. The practice of digital twin technology in the oil and gas industry is a relatively innovative area of research and development, and there is still much to be learned about how to effectively implement this technology and leverage it to achieve sustainability goals. While there is some existing literature on the use of digital twin technology, much of this paper has focused on the digital twin solution in a comprehensive platform leveraging machine learning algorithms that can connect with a plenty of data sources to provide real-time visibility into asset performance, enabling them to optimize operations, reduce emissions, and better manage environmental risks.

Authors: B. Bąk, Jakub Wilk, Piotr Artiemjew, J. Wilde
Title: Recording the Presence of Peanibacillus larvae larvae Colonies on MYPGP Substrates Using a Multi-Sensor Array Based on Solid-State Gas Sensors
Abstract: American foulbrood is a dangerous disease of bee broods found worldwide, caused by the Paenibacillus larvae larvae L. bacterium. In an experiment, the possibility of detecting colonies of this bacterium on MYPGP substrates (which contains yeast extract, Mueller-Hinton broth, glucose, K2HPO4, sodium pyruvate, and agar) was tested using a prototype of a multi-sensor recorder of the MCA-8 sensor signal with a matrix of six semiconductors: TGS 823, TGS 826, TGS 832, TGS 2600, TGS 2602, and TGS 2603 from Figaro. Two twin prototypes of the MCA-8 measurement device, M1 and M2, were used in the study. Each prototype was attached to two laboratory test chambers: a wooden one and a polystyrene one. For the experiment, the strain used was P. l. larvae ATCC 9545, ERIC I. On MYPGP medium, often used for laboratory diagnosis of American foulbrood, this bacterium produces small, transparent, smooth, and shiny colonies. Gas samples from over culture media of one- and two-day-old foulbrood P. l. larvae (with no colonies visible to the naked eye) and from over culture media older than 2 days (with visible bacterial colonies) were examined. In addition, the air from empty chambers was tested. The measurement time was 20 min, including a 10-min testing exposure phase and a 10-min sensor regeneration phase. The results were analyzed in two variants: without baseline correction and with baseline correction. We tested 14 classifiers and found that a prototype of a multi-sensor recorder of the MCA-8 sensor signal was capable of detecting colonies of P. l. larvae on MYPGP substrate with a 97% efficiency and could distinguish between MYPGP substrates with 1–2 days of culture, and substrates with older cultures. The efficacy of copies of the prototypes M1 and M2 was shown to differ slightly. The weighted method with Canberra metrics (Canberra.811) and kNN with Canberra and Manhattan metrics (Canberra. 1nn and manhattan.1nn) proved to be the most effective classifiers.

Authors: Fengchun Tian, Xiang Fu, Haibing Wang, Jingya Zhang, Hao-Ran Gao, Shu-Kai Duan, Li-Dan Wang, Min Tian
Title: NORP: A Compact Neuromorphic Olfactory Recognition Processor With On-Chip Hybrid Learning
Source: 2023 IEEE International Conference on Integrated Circuits, Technologies and Applications (ICTA)
Abstract: This work proposes a low-cost neuromorphic olfactory recognition processor for electronic noses. The processor targets a two-layer spiking neural network, enabling on-chip unsupervised spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) learning for the feature extraction layer and supervised spike-error dependent plasticity (SEDP) learning for the feature classification layer. An FPGA prototype of the SNN processor was implemented. It attained a comparably high accuracy of 96.25% at a 188 sample/s inference speed on the Twin Gas Sensor Arrays odor dataset.

Authors: Vishakha Pareek, S. Chaudhury, Sanjay Singh
Title: Gas Discrimination & Quantification using Sensor Array with 3D Convolution Regression Dual Network
Source: 2021 11th IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Data Acquisition and Advanced Computing Systems: Technology and Applications (IDAACS)
Abstract: Smart sensor system design requires intelligent data processing, which analyzes raw time-series sensor data to efficiently and precisely discriminate and quantify target gases. The work presented here utilizes the response of twin gas sensor arrays for gases such as ethanol, ethylene, methane, and carbon monoxide to discriminate and quantify the target gases. We propose a 3D convolution neural-based regression dual network (3D-CNRDN) for both gas quantification and discrimination. The spatiotemporal correlation of sensor array responses inspired us to design the deep neural network for the gas concentration estimation model. The sensor array set is spatially correlated, and all the twin array responses are temporally related. 3D-CNRDN uses raw time-series gas sensor array data. The data is fed to the network as the 3D pattern, which contains 2D spatial information varying with third dimension time to recognize patterns that eventually predict the concentration. The model evaluation shows that the proposed methods are an effective technique for gas quantification and identification with $\text{RMSE}=0.3179$ and classification accuracy 94.37%. Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms and provides higher discrimination accuracy and lower RMSE than other machine learning and deep learning methods.

Authors: R. Choens, Kristopher Kuhlman, C. Herrick, S. Otto
Title: Acoustic Emission Monitoring of Thermal Cycling in Salt at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant
Source: Proceedings 56th US Rock Mechanics / Geomechanics Symposium
Abstract: A series of field-based multi-physics observations were conducted as part of the Brine Availability Test in Salt (BATS) underground at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP), near Carlsbad, NM. Observations were made of brine production, temperature, electrical resistivity, acoustic emissions (AE), and gas/liquid tracer migration through salt around twin heated/unheated borehole arrays. Here, we present AE results from thermal cycling experiments performed May – July 2021, during which the heater was pulsed several times followed by two longer heated periods. Sixteen AE sensors were installed in three parallel observational boreholes surrounding the central heated borehole. Observed AE demonstrate that heating and cooling cycles significantly impact salt behavior. AE rates increased during heating and increased further upon cooling. Average energy and frequency bandwidth also increased during heating and cooling of salt. Similar behavior was observed for each heating/cooling cycle, suggesting that temperature-enhanced salt healing may have eliminated any threshold loading associated with the onset of AE (i.e., the Kaiser effect). Locations of AE events remained centralized around the borehole. These results show that AE provide valuable information about the thermal behavior of salt, particularly that cooling of salt results in the highest AE behavior.

Authors: Abdul Shakoor, Syed Adil Sardar, Almas, W. Kim, Shahzad Iqbal
Title: Emerging Trends in Single-Atom Engineered Materials for Intelligent Gas Sensing: Materials Design, Machine Learning, and Future Opportunities
Abstract: Intelligent gas sensors (IGSs) have garnered significant attention owing to their highly sensitive, selective, and reliable gas detection in industrial safety, environmental monitoring, food quality assessment, healthcare diagnostics, and smart Internet of Things (IoT) frameworks. While traditional metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) gas sensors demonstrate exceptional sensitivity and cost-effective fabrication, their practical implementation is typically hindered by slow recovery, poor selectivity, long-term instability, and susceptibility to environmental interference. In recent times, single-atom engineered materials, specifically single-atom catalysts (SACs), have attracted considerable attention because isolated metal atoms maximize atomic utilization efficiency while providing highly uniform and well-defined catalytic active sites. These exceptional atomic-scale properties substantially enhance charge transfer, gas adsorption, surface reaction kinetics, and catalytic activity, resulting in marked improvements in sensing performance. At the same time, the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has transformed traditional gas sensors into smart sensing technologies with optimized pattern recognition, feature extraction, gas classification, concentration prediction, drift compensation, and instantaneous decision-making. In this review, we have comprehensively summarized the recent advancements in single-atom engineered materials for smart gas sensing. The fundamental sensing mechanisms of single-atom materials, such as electronic structure engineering, adsorption modulation, and catalytic activation, are first discussed. Afterward, recent progress in SA-supported MOs gas sensors (SAC/MO-GSs) is thoroughly addressed, with special focus on SA classification, anchoring and stabilization strategies, metal–support interactions, and their impact on catalytic reactions, gas adsorption, charge transfer, and sensing performance. The incorporation of ML algorithms-such as random forests (RF), support vector machines (SVMs), k-nearest neighbors (k-NNs), principal component analysis (PCA), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and deep learning architectures-for smart gas sensing and sensor-array design is critically examined. Additionally, current challenges relating to atomic stability, scalable synthesis, data availability, computational cost, model generalization, practical device integration, and long-term durability are reviewed alongside emerging prospects in explainable AI, edge computing, digital twins, and self-powered wearable sensing devices. In conclusion, we have proposed future research directions toward the design of next-generation smart gas sensors that integrate atomic-scale sensing material engineering along with cutting-edge artificial intelligence, offering a route toward low-power, accurate, and autonomous gas-sensing applications.

Authors: Jing-Xiao Li, Ling-Wei Yu, Hai Yang, Zhe Wang
Title: Discrete wavelet transform and multi-scale parallel convolutional network for gas recognition
Abstract: Electronic nose (e-nose) systems based on metal oxide sensor arrays are widely deployed in food safety, environmental monitoring, and medical diagnosis. However, accurate gas identification remains challenging due to two factors: (1) most deep learning methods insufficiently exploit the transient dynamics of sensor response signals, discarding critical time-frequency information; (2) the limited receptive fields of standard convolutional neural networks hinder the modelling of long-range dependencies across sensor channels and temporal evolution. To address these issues, we propose a discrete wavelet transform and multi-scale parallel convolutional network (DWT-MPCN) that formulates gas recognition as a time-frequency image classification problem. Specifically, a fixed five-level db5 discrete wavelet transform (DWT) module converts multi-channel raw time-domain signals into two-dimensional wavelet coefficient maps without manual feature engineering, preserving both rapid transient details and slow recovery trends. A Multi-scale Parallel Convolution (MPC) module then employs parallel convolutional branches with different kernel sizes to simultaneously capture local transient features and broader contextual patterns while maintaining a lightweight architecture (only 1.75 M parameters). Finally, a convolutional Transformer encoder adaptively weights cross-sensor and cross-scale features to produce discriminative representations. Evaluated on three public e-nose datasets with distinct sensor configurations and gas types, DWT-MPCN achieves mean accuracies of 99.69±0.10% on the OPEN SAMPLING dataset, 99.11±0.16% on the TWIN dataset, and 99.82±0.11% on the large-scale array sensor dataset across five independently seeded runs. Component ablations, capacity-aware comparisons, hyperparameter analyses, and wavelet-parameter sensitivity studies validate the contribution of each component and clarify the design choices. The proposed method provides a compact and interpretable framework for edge-intelligent olfaction systems. Our supporting code is publicly available at https://github.com/ECUSTLiJingxiao/DWT-MPCN-support.

Authors: Kiran More, Yashwardhan Desale, Yash Dhaktode, Prachi Pawar
Title: A Smart Industrial Safety Helmet with Continuous Health Monitoring and 3D Visualization
Source: 2026 Conference on Latest Innovations in Computing and Knowledge (CLICK)
Abstract: This paper provides an overview of an advanced safety helmet incorporating both physiological and environmental sensors and integrating with edge and cloud computing infrastructure, data processing techniques and realtime monitoring interface. The helmet consists of an array of sensors measuring heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, ambient environmental (temperature and humidity) conditions, gases, motion and usage, which then have data sent via lowpower wireless protocols (Wi-Fi / LoRa / Bluetooth, etc.), to both edge nodes and cloud servers for monitoring and logging purposes as well as generating alerts in real-time. A 3D digital twin online dashboard is used to visualize and display the sensor data. The paper describes the overall system architecture, sensor integration, and implementation of the entire system using a ThingBoard-type IoT platform. As part of the overall safety goals, gas exposure alerting, heat stress warning and fall detection safety use cases are outside of our current prototype and will use the proposed predictive analytics framework, which can model health risks based on vital sign trends. Reliable data was generated and responsiveness of the integrated features validated through simulated scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of using smart PPE to enhance worker safety within the industrial environment..

Authors: H. Jin, W. Liu
Title: Physics-Informed Digital Framework for Emissions Characterization and Use-Case Applications
Source: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
Abstract: Emissions quantification and production surveillance are commonly implemented as separate measurement workflows, relying on dedicated gas sensors, intrusive instrumentation, or periodic surveys that are difficult to scale across heterogeneous facilities and changing operating conditions. This paper presents a physics-informed emissions-quantification framework that couples upstream fuel metering with remote atmospheric inversion to reconstruct facility-level carbon flux continuously. The present study validates the framework for carbon dioxide (CO2); methane-specific detection and quantification performance are not evaluated. The framework is implemented as a digital twin that embeds mass conservation, combustion stoichiometry, and advection-diffusion transport within a physics-informed neural network (PINN) architecture. Facility emissions are represented as latent source terms in a constrained mass-balance formulation. Emission rates are inferred from residual structure between (i) measured fuel input and thermodynamically consistent inventory/outlet states and (ii) atmosphere-derived concentration fields. The formulation accounts for measurement sparsity, sensor noise, and transient atmospheric variability while enforcing physical consistency and reporting observability diagnostics. Field testing was conducted during 2025 at an operating industrial manufacturing facility under building-scale flow obstruction, variable wind, and complex plume transport. A 12-station distributed sensing array spanning approximately 11 m end to end across a rooftop transect measured CO2 and volatile organic compound (VOC) concentration gradients during controlled-combustion and controlled-release scenarios. Upstream fuel input was quantified using metering augmented by PINN-based estimation to provide the process-side carbon reference used in the coupled estimator. Two evaluations were kept distinct: controlled CO2 releases, for which the meter-side constraint was omitted and release metadata were withheld, provided an independent end-to-end check of the sensing-and-inversion chain; the full-year atmosphere-versus-fuel comparison assessed closed-loop consistency because the fuel-derived reference was included as a soft training constraint. Twenty controlled CO2 releases from calibrated cylinders, conducted at 0.5–40 kg/h from three source locations within a 10 m radius, yielded a maximum absolute relative error of 10.3% (mean 5.5%), a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of approximately 1.0 kg/h, and R2 = 0.992. In the 2025 closed-loop comparison, monthly signed differences for months with a nonzero fuel reference were bounded within ±14.5%, while the annual aggregate atmosphere-versus-fuel difference was +6.8%. The controlled-release and supplementary characterization set covered 0–45 km/h; the broader full-year field record spanned 3–58 km/h, and the 0–1 km/h calm bin was laboratory-only. Descriptive wind-bin means showed the smallest absolute bias (≤4%) from 12 to 38 km/h. Because within-bin sample counts and dispersion were unavailable for this analysis, that range is presented as a provisional low-bias regime rather than a statistically validated operating envelope. All reported accuracy results are CO2-specific. Methane deployment requires methane-sensitive instrumentation, controlled methane releases, and site-specific qualification.

Authors: D. Raka, P. Srivastava, A. Mohamed
Title: Real-Time Health Monitoring and Surrogate Sensor Solutions for MPFMs
Abstract: Multiphase flow meters (MPFM) provide real-time measurement of well production rate including oil, water and gas phase fractions. This real-time data is crucial for making operational decisions and managing reservoirs effectively. An MPFM typically incorporates an array of critical sensors, including those for measuring flow velocity, determining gas–oil ratio (GOR), assessing water cut (WCUT), and monitoring operating pressure (P) and temperature (T). These measurements provide essential parameters for accurate calculations under prevailing operating conditions. This paper introduces a novel technology for real-time health assessment of MPFMs by applying advanced diagnostics to sensor raw data and presents a proprietary digital twin of the MPFM for continuous health monitoring and root-cause analysis. It also details surrogate methods to compensate for critical sensor failures. The primary objective is to continuously monitor MPFM health, preventing incorrect allocations and decisions based on faulty readings. Furthermore, the technology provides surrogate for malfunctioning sensors and utilizes an in-house proprietary MPFM digital twin to utilize data from functioning sensors and estimate well rates instead of rendering the entire meter inoperative due to few sensor failures. The methodology for diagnosing meter health involves real-time data collection and applying diagnostics to assess individual sensor health. Alerts are generated based on the issue's criticality and displayed in a format easily understandable by field engineers. The digital twin is leveraged for root cause analysis whenever a discrepancy in MPFM behavior is observed. For each sensor type, a specific surrogate has been identified and tested, based on an understanding of how that sensor affects meter rate estimations. These surrogates, combined with data from functioning sensors, are used in the MPFM twin to estimate phase flow rates during partial sensor failures. Implementation of this technology has significantly improved MPFM monitoring and maintenance. Field engineers report that the diagnostics system enables early issue detection and timely intervention. Despite partial failures in MPFM, the surrogate methods have facilitated the estimation of well fluid composition with the best achievable precision, leading to better well allocation and more informed decisions on production strategy. This work presents a novel real-time diagnostics framework for MPFMs that addresses a key challenge in field operations—meters continuing to output flow rates even when sensor data is faulty, such as flatlined or out-of-bounds values. The proposed system continuously analyzes raw sensor data and generates near real-time health alerts, enabling early detection of sensor degradation or failure. When discrepancies in MPFM behavior are detected, the digital twin facilitates faster root cause analysis and serves as a proxy for the meter until corrections are implemented. In cases where critical sensors malfunction, the system employs surrogate sensors within the digital twin to estimate flow rates using data from the remaining functional sensors. This approach enables continued use of partial sensor information to derive meaningful well rate estimates, rather than discarding all data due to a single point of failure, thereby improving reliability and decision-making in production operations.
